query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy develops a higher degree of local chemical short‐range order (SRO) and concomitant lattice distortions than its quaternary and ternary subsets, which in turn increases the barrier to dislocation glide. This enhanced dislocation pinning contributes to higher yield strength and strain hardening during deformation despite similar overall phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single‐phase FCC alloys (quinary, quaternary, and ternary subsets) produced by identical thermomechanical processing.
generation.intervention: Prepare controlled alloy batches in which one element is systematically removed (to form quaternary and ternary alloys) while keeping processing and microstructure (FCC single phase) constant, followed by mechanical tensile (or compression) testing.
generation.conditions: Deformation tests conducted at room temperature (and optionally at a controlled sub‐room temperature) under the same strain rate, ensuring that temperature and strain rate effects are held constant across the comparisons.
generation.structural_mediator: The extent and distribution of local chemical short‐range order and the resulting lattice distortions.
generation.mechanism: Increased compositional complexity in the quinary alloy fosters stronger and spatially heterogeneous SRO that increases lattice distortions. These local structural features act as barriers to dislocation motion, effectively increasing resistance to slip, delaying dynamic recovery, and promoting a higher strain hardening response. In contrast, the reduced complexity in quaternary and ternary subsets leads to less pronounced SRO and diminished barrier effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical testing conditions, the quinary alloy will display a higher yield strength and work hardening rate, along with delayed necking or failure, compared to its quaternary and ternary counterparts.
generation.baseline: The mechanical performance (yield strength, strain hardening behavior, ductility) of the fully equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy under the specified test conditions serves as the reference point.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to thermomechanically processed, single-phase FCC structures tested under similar temperatures (e.g., room temperature) and strain rates; results outside these conditions (e.g., drastically different temperatures or phase changes) may not follow the predicted behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While there is supporting evidence that SRO and lattice distortion can influence dislocation mobility in HEAs, the quantitative contribution of these factors relative to other possible mechanisms (e.g., stacking fault energy variations or impurity segregation effects) remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a set of equiatomic FCC samples: one quinary (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni), and controlled quaternary and ternary subsets (removing one or two elements at a time while maintaining single-phase FCC microstructures). Conduct tensile tests at a fixed room temperature and constant strain rate while characterizing local SRO/lattice distortion with high-resolution TEM and/or atom probe tomography.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of local chemical order (e.g., SRO parameters) and lattice distortion distributions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quinary alloy does not show significantly higher yield strength and work hardening compared to the quaternary and ternary alloys, or if high-resolution microstructural analysis reveals no statistically significant difference in the degree of SRO or lattice distortions between the quinary and lower constituent count alloys, then the hypothesis that enhanced SRO and lattice distortion mediates the property differences is falsified.

The yield stress of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA increases significantly as the temperature is decreased from room temperature to 77 K. The strong negative temperature dependence of yield stress is due to the thermal component of solid-solution hardening and not due to significantly different mobilities of the edge and screw dislocation segments, as is evident from the absence of preferred orientations for dislocations introduced during deformation at low temperatures. This behavior is similar to that of typical FCC metals and different from that of many BCC metals. Most dislocations are confined to their original slip planes forming a planar arrangement without significant cross-slip at low strains. The perfect dislocation in the HEA is observed to dissociate into two Shockley partial dislocations with a stacking fault in between. The stacking fault energy of the HEA deduced from the separation distance of the two, coupled, Shockley partial dislocations is 30 ± 5 mJ/m2, which is relatively low but not particularly so when compared with certain FCC metals and alloys. Although the stacking fault energy is not particularly low, the separation distance between the Shockley partials can be large

Recently, Ding et al. synthesized FCC CoCrFeNiPd and CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. The former exhibited a higher yield strength than the latter with comparable tensile ductility. They proposed that the essential difference between these two HEAs was associated with atomic segregation and short-range ordering (SRO); both were enhanced in CoCrFeNiPd, as compared with CoCrFeNiMn. The idea was that SRO tends to create resistance to deformation/slip, leading to larger dislocation glide resistance in the more ordered CoCrFeNiPd than in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. Theoretical work by Yin et al. suggested that the strengthening was due mainly to the large atomic/misfit volume of Pd in CoCrFeNi. Ma et al. identified a number of unusual features associated with dislocations/slips in HEAs that were related to lattice distortion and/or local chemical order. SRO also occurs in medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). The atomic structure of a CoCrNi MEA indicates that Cr favors Ni and Co neighbors, reducing the electrical and thermal conductivities and increasing the stacking-fault energies and hardness.
